extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / Royal Society readers (17th-century scientists, astronomers, botanists, experimentalists)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and expectations for reporting experiments, observations, and book-reviews in 17th-century natural philosophy: how to collect and describe specimens, design and report experiments, use historical and experiential corroboration, and articulate hypotheses about natural phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Botanical catalogue: direct collection and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Author should travel and personally view and gather plants from all considerable parts of the kingdom where feasible; compare gathered specimens diligently with histories and figures from other botanists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘he has spared neither pains nor cost, travelling himself through all the considerable parts of this kingdom, and so viewing and gathering himself almost all the plants here described…diligently compared them with their histories and figures found by botanists.’ Use first-hand collection wherever possible; when specimens are taken from other authors or friends, state sources and compare critically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Botanical catalogue: corrective and comprehensive description
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide synonyma, summary descriptions of principal virtues, characteristic notes, and correct previous omissions and confusions in the literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reader should find ‘the most necessary synonyma…a summary description also of their principal virtues; intermixed with many new observations and experiments…describing those which seemed to have been omitted by others, and adding…those that had been confusedly and carelessly delivered before.’ Include medicinal/physiological observations where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Book assessment: evaluate plan, execution, and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful review assesses whether the author's plan and execution facilitate the intended knowledge or practice, noting when complexity impedes usability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example critique: Ray's Historia Plantarum is ‘complex and intricate’ and ‘neither the plan nor the execution is in any degree calculated to facilitate the knowledge of plants.’ Discuss both intellectual ambition and practical accessibility for intended readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental control and reporting (mites experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe experimental apparatus and procedures precisely (e.g., exhausted portable receiver, secured from regress of air), record durations, and report observable outcomes before and after manipulation (e.g., admission of air).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report how samples were kept (from Monday morning to Thursday morning), what was observed (no signs of life until air let in), and outcomes (mites resumed motion). Provide enough procedural detail to allow readers to judge controls and potential confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration and rebuttal of alternative hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate alternative explanations (e.g., spontaneous generation) and evaluate their plausibility against known facts and difficulty of the proposed mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author rejects spontaneous generation for mites in vacuo ‘because of the extreme difficulty of making any living creature to be generated in vacuo…’ Use life-cycle knowledge and prior observations of eggs/seasonality to argue against alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish regular (statistical) causes from accidental contingencies
rubrics_metrics.description: When proposing periodic explanations (diurnal, menstrual, annual), explicitly separate regular, repeatable causes from accidental/extrinsic influences like wind or land-water runoff, and state when such contingencies are precluded from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘I did…preclude the consideration of the advantage or disadvantage which should arise from such uncertain contingencies, which was wholly beside my business; which was to give a statical account of stated periods.’ Make assumptions explicit and restrict claims to the intended scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical records and experiential testimony as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Corroborate observational claims with chronicles, historical instances, and the long-standing practical experience of practitioners (e.g., seamen), citing dates and accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author draws on Holinshed, Stow, chronicles and named dates (e.g., 1250, 1555) and seamen's testimony about wind effects. Use such documentary evidence to support causal inferences while noting their limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult domain practitioners (seamen) and incorporate local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek and report the judgments and habitual observations of experienced local practitioners (seamen, watermen) about phenomena (e.g., times and wind directions associated with high tides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The letter repeatedly appeals to seamen of Kent, Weymouth, Rochester for practical knowledge (e.g., north-west wind makes highest tides). Treat practitioner testimony as valuable empirical input to hypotheses and observation campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and document measurements precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Record quantitative measurements with appropriate units and precision (e.g., magnetic declination given in degrees and minutes), and report changes over time with dates and comparators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hevelius reports declination changed from ~3°5' to 7°20' over 28 years and cites other observers' measurements. Provide numeric measures, dates, and comparisons to enable assessment of magnitude and trend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal and geographically distributed observation campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish regularities or bounds of variation, collect accurate observations over many years and across multiple places; propose and coordinate targeted observations at strategic locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘the accurate observations of the subsequent years will show how far this deflexion will proceed…’ and calls for observations at Bristol and year-round measurements at Weymouth. Recommend coordinated, sustained measurement programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis testing via targeted predictions and observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Derive testable, location- and time-specific predictions from hypotheses (e.g., when and where tides should be higher) and prescribe concrete observations to confirm or refute them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author requests observation whether ‘the spring tides be not sensibly higher after the change than after the full in February, March and April’ and similar month-by-month predictions. Formulate specific observational checks tied to the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theoretical modeling must combine relevant celestial motions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain periodic earthly phenomena by combining the relevant celestial motions (diurnal, menstrual, annual) and orbital properties (eccentricity, obliquity, perigee/apogee) rather than attributing them to single isolated causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Wallis explains how compositions of diurnal, menstrual, and annual motions give tides; includes consideration of earth/moon common centre of gravity, eccentricity and obliquity. Models should account for combined effects and explain phase relationships (e.g., spring/neap timings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude or set aside accidental extrinsic factors when presenting statical accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: When the aim is to present a statical theory of periodicity, explicitly exclude extrinsic accidental factors (wind, storms, land-water runoff) from the model and note that they can produce exceptional events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘I did…preclude the consideration of the advantage or disadvantage which should arise from such uncertain contingencies…’ When doing so, state this assumption clearly and acknowledge that it limits applicability to non-accidental cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple independent lines of evidence and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims by combining empirical observation, historical examples, practitioner testimony, and theoretical argument rather than relying on a single type of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the letters, the correspondents cite observations, chronicles, seamen, and celestial mechanics together. Present corroboration from varied sources to strengthen inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report experimental and observational limitations and locality-specific variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge when phenomena vary by locale (coasts differ), season, or when records are incomplete, and refrain from overgeneralizing from localized observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note that effects on Romney Marsh need not be identical at Weymouth or other coasts and that ‘what variety is on other coasts I am not certain.’ State geographic/temporal limits of claims and where further measurement is needed.
